# Nara Notes

## Overview

Two nights in Nara, in from Osaka on the Kintetsu line rather than the slower national service, and staying in a small guesthouse near Naramachi. I dropped my bag at midday, took the bus north and walked the park before the afternoon crowds built. The town is small enough to cross on foot in an evening, and almost everything I wanted lay inside a band of parkland and old streets. I gave the first day to the deer and the second to gardens and shops.

Rain held off until the last morning, when the whole town smelled of wet cedar. I chose two nights because one would have meant rushing the temples and never seeing Naramachi in daylight, and that choice was right. The second evening I ate early, walked the lantern-lit lanes south of the main road and was back at the guesthouse by nine. The deer are the reason many people come, but the quiet of the east side after dark is what stayed with me. I would stay in the same area again, close to the shops and away from the station noise. The guesthouse had eight rooms, a shared bath and a kettle in the corridor, and it cost me 7200 yen a night.

## Food

Naramachi is where I ate, and the small places near the covered market were better than anything around the station. The first night I found a counter shop with six stools and ordered the local pressed sushi, wrapped in persimmon leaf, five pieces for 1200 yen. The fish was mackerel, cured just long enough to firm up, and it came with a cup of clear soup. Breakfast was a set at the guesthouse: rice, miso, a grilled fillet and pickles, and it held me until mid-afternoon.

The mochi pounding street is short and loud, one shop after another working rice with wooden mallets and selling the result warm. I watched a pair take turns for ten minutes, the rhythm steady, and bought two pieces for 250 yen. They were softer than any mochi I had eaten before and gone in a few bites. Midday I took a bowl of udon near the park gate, thick noodles in a dark broth with a slab of fried tofu, for 900 yen. The second evening I went back to the market arcade and had grilled skewers and a small bottle of sake, about 2100 yen for the lot. Matcha soft-serve from a shop on the way back was 400 yen and worth the queue. I drank mostly tea and water, which kept the food bill low. The teahouse near the garden served a set of matcha and a sweet for 700 yen, and I sat over it while the afternoon cooled. Vegetarian food is uncommon in the old shops, so I ate fish most meals and did not mind. One evening I joined a queue for a bowl of hot noodles behind the station, 800 yen, and it was the plainest and best meal of the stay.

## Notes

The Isuien garden was the best hour of the trip and almost empty on a weekday morning. It uses the borrowed scenery of the temple roofs and the wooded hill behind, so the view feels far larger than the plot. Entry was 1200 yen with the small museum next door, and I sat on the veranda for a long while watching carp work the pond. The deer are persistent around the food stalls and will nose at a bag if you let them. I kept snacks zipped away and bought the deer crackers only in the open. Bus stops are frequent and a day pass covers the park loop. Cash worked everywhere, cards almost nowhere. I left on the early train with the wet smell of the trees still in my coat. The museum beside the garden is small and has a good collection of old maps and screens, and I spent twenty minutes there out of the rain. The temples east of the park are quieter than the great hall and mostly free, and I walked between three of them on the second morning. A bus pass costs 500 yen for the day, which I bought twice. The tourist office at the station gave me a good paper map and marked the current closures, which the phone app had not updated.
